derived_from_data.tilt_note: Consistent across all three frames. Most likely the raised scanner head looking down rather than the can leaning. Harmless here: it tips the axis within the y-z plane, which stays perpendicular to x, so shear visibility stayed at 0.994.

conditions.distance_note: The owner's 120 is a rough desk measurement against a raised scanner head and was NOT used in any calculation. The fit reads the radius off the point cloud and the scanner supplies every z, so an inaccurate standoff estimate cannot bias the diameter.
conditions.surface: BARE, untreated, specular aluminium - deliberately unsprayed

measured_result.verdict_reason: A shear was detected, so the harness declines to attribute the -0.295 to scale rather than to the shear. That is the correct outcome, not an evasion.

target.note: The can body measures a consistent 58 around the middle. The top and bottom are flanged and stand proud of the body, but at this distance they fall outside the vertical field of view and return nothing, so no cropping was applied.

what: Depth frames of a drink can captured for METRIC VALIDATION. Unlike the frames in tests/fixtures/frames/, these have an independently measured ground truth.
what_this_does_NOT_establish: Whether the residual -0.295 is a scale error or the detected shear. One view cannot separate them, which is why the verdict is inconclusive.
Any distortion model. The deprojection is an ideal pinhole.
what_this_establishes: The depth scale is MILLIMETRES. 57.7 against 58.0 rules out any other unit by orders of magnitude. That scalar was unknown for the entire prior life of this project.

The factory cx near 42 is approximately right. A shear was detected but its coefficient is about -0.026, where cx belonging at the frame centre would give -0.309 - twelve times larger. The off-centre principal point is a real property of the sensor.
A bare specular surface is not a blocker: 40% yield, the highest of any frame in this repository, and a frame-to-frame spread of 0.044.
